lessons.title: API docs, contracts, SDKs and reviews
lessons.summary: OpenAPI 3.1 design-first versus code-first, linting and breaking-change checks, SDK generation, consumer-driven contract testing with Pact, and running API design reviews.
lessons.body:
## The core idea
An API is a contract between teams that may never talk to each other. The contract has to exist somewhere other than in the server's code and the client author's head, otherwise every change is a guess and every integration starts with reading source code. Mature API teams treat the contract as a first-class artefact:

- **Described** in a machine-readable spec (OpenAPI for HTTP/JSON, protobuf for gRPC, the SDL for GraphQL, AsyncAPI for events).
- **Checked** automatically: linted for style, diffed for breaking changes, and verified against the running implementation.
- **Consumed** through generated documentation, SDKs, mocks and tests, so the spec cannot silently drift.
- **Reviewed** by people before it ships, because the expensive mistakes in APIs are design mistakes you cannot fix later.

## OpenAPI in practice
OpenAPI 3.1 describes HTTP APIs in YAML or JSON: paths, operations, parameters, request and response bodies, auth schemes and reusable schemas. 3.1 aligned its schema objects with JSON Schema 2020-12, so the same schemas can validate payloads at runtime.

```yaml
openapi: 3.1.0
info: { title: Orders API, version: "2026-10-01" }
servers: [{ url: https://api.example.com/v1 }]
security: [{ bearerAuth: [] }]
paths:
  /orders:
    post:
      operationId: createOrder
      parameters:
        - { name: Idempotency-Key, in: header, required: true, schema: { type: string, maxLength: 255 } }
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema: { $ref: "#/components/schemas/CreateOrder" }
      responses:
        "201":
          description: Created
          headers: { Location: { schema: { type: string } } }
          content: { application/json: { schema: { $ref: "#/components/schemas/Order" } } }
        "422": { $ref: "#/components/responses/Problem" }
        "429": { $ref: "#/components/responses/Problem" }
components:
  securitySchemes:
    bearerAuth: { type: http, scheme: bearer }
  schemas:
    CreateOrder:
      type: object
      required: [customer_id, items]
      properties:
        customer_id: { type: string, pattern: "^cus_" }
        items: { type: array, minItems: 1, maxItems: 100, items: { $ref: "#/components/schemas/LineItem" } }
    Order:
      type: object
      required: [id, status, total]
      properties:
        id: { type: string, examples: ["ord_8f2c"] }
        status: { type: string, enum: [pending, paid, shipped, cancelled], description: "Open enum: handle unknown values." }
        total: { $ref: "#/components/schemas/Money" }
  responses:
    Problem:
      description: RFC 9457 problem details
      content: { application/problem+json: { schema: { $ref: "#/components/schemas/Problem" } } }
```

### Design-first versus code-first
- **Design-first**: write (or generate from a higher-level language like TypeSpec) the spec, review it as a pull request, then implement against it. Reviewers see the contract without reading handler code, frontend and backend can build in parallel against a mock server, and the spec is the source of truth. Cost: you must keep the implementation honest, so add request and response validation middleware or contract tests that fail when code and spec differ.
- **Code-first**: generate the spec from code annotations or schemas (FastAPI from Pydantic models, NestJS decorators, zod schemas through a generator). Always in sync with what the code does, faster for small teams. Cost: the API design is shaped by framework convenience, and reviewers only see the contract after it is implemented.

A pragmatic middle path that many teams land on: code-first from runtime schemas (so one zod or Pydantic definition drives validation and the spec), with the **generated spec committed to the repo** so every pull request shows a reviewable contract diff, plus lint and breaking-change checks on that diff.

### Tooling around the spec
- **Linting**: Spectral rulesets encode your style guide (casing, pagination parameters, required `operationId`, problem-details errors, no verbs in paths) and fail CI.
- **Breaking-change detection**: diff the spec against the last released version (oasdiff for OpenAPI, `buf breaking` for protobuf, schema checks for GraphQL) and block removals and type changes unless the change is explicitly versioned.
- **Docs**: rendered from the spec (Redoc, Scalar, Swagger UI) with real examples, plus hand-written guides for authentication, pagination, errors, idempotency and webhooks. The reference tells you what each field is; the guides tell you how to accomplish a task.
- **Mocks**: a mock server from the spec (Prism is a common one) lets frontend teams and partners start before the backend exists.
- **Fuzzing**: Schemathesis generates property-based tests from the spec and finds 500s, schema violations and crashes on edge-case inputs.

## SDK generation
Most developers integrate through an SDK, not raw HTTP. Generating SDKs from the spec keeps them in sync, but generated code is only as good as the spec and the generator:

- `openapi-typescript` generates TypeScript types from a spec; paired with a small typed fetch client it gives compile-time checked calls with almost no runtime cost.
- `openapi-generator` covers dozens of languages with variable quality.
- Commercial generators (Stainless, Speakeasy, Fern) produce idiomatic SDKs with retries, pagination helpers and typed errors; Stainless generates the official OpenAI and Anthropic SDKs, for example.

A good SDK handles what every client gets wrong by hand: auth, retries with backoff for retryable errors, automatic idempotency keys on POST, auto-pagination iterators, typed errors from problem details, timeouts, and forward compatibility (unknown enum values and fields must not throw).

```ts
import createClient from "openapi-fetch";
import type { paths } from "./generated/orders-api"; // from: npx openapi-typescript openapi.yaml -o ...

const api = createClient<paths>({ baseUrl: "https://api.example.com/v1", headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` } });

const { data, error } = await api.POST("/orders", {
  params: { header: { "Idempotency-Key": crypto.randomUUID() } },
  body: { customer_id: "cus_1", items: [{ sku: "sku_9", quantity: 2 }] },   // type-checked against the spec
});
if (error) console.error(error.title);   // typed problem details
```

## Contract testing with Pact
End-to-end tests across many services are slow, flaky and need every service deployed together. **Consumer-driven contract testing** (Ian Robinson's article on martinfowler.com introduced the idea) replaces most of them:

```text
CONSUMER (web app) test                     PROVIDER (orders service) CI
  - runs against a Pact mock server          - fetches pacts for its consumers from the broker
  - records: "GET /orders/ord_1 ->            - replays each interaction against the real provider
     200 {id, status}"                          (with provider states: "order ord_1 exists")
  - writes a pact file (JSON contract)        - publishes verification results
        |                                              |
        +--------------> Pact Broker <-----------------+
                              |
              can-i-deploy?  checks the matrix of versions before each deploy
```

What it buys you: each consumer states exactly which fields and interactions it relies on, the provider learns precisely which changes would break which consumer, and `can-i-deploy` prevents shipping an incompatible pair. It is consumer-driven: the provider is free to change anything no consumer uses.

When it is worth it: many internal services and teams with independent deploys, where integration breakage is a recurring cost. When it is not: a single team owning both sides (a typed shared client or a monorepo type check is enough), or public APIs with unknown consumers (use spec-based breaking-change checks and versioning instead). Pact also has a learning curve (provider states, broker hosting, versioning conventions). PactFlow's bi-directional contract testing compares consumer pacts against the provider's OpenAPI spec instead of replaying against the provider, which suits teams that already maintain a validated spec.

## API reviews
An API design review before implementation is the cheapest place to catch problems. Google's API design guide, Microsoft's REST API guidelines and Zalando's guidelines are effectively public checklists. A review should answer:

1. **Model**: are the resources the right nouns? Will this shape still make sense when the feature grows (multiple currencies, multiple addresses, teams instead of users)?
2. **Consistency**: naming, casing, pagination, filtering, errors and ids match the rest of the API.
3. **Evolution**: are enums documented as open, are booleans going to need a third state, is anything exposing internal implementation (database ids, table names)?
4. **Safety**: idempotency for writes, rate limits, authorisation per resource (not just per endpoint), limits on payload sizes and list lengths.
5. **Operations**: async shape for slow work, webhooks for events, observability (request ids), deprecation path.
6. **Developer experience**: can a new developer accomplish the main task from the docs in 15 minutes? Are examples realistic?

Keep reviews lightweight (a written proposal plus the spec diff, reviewed asynchronously by a small group that owns the guidelines) and automate everything mechanical with linting, so humans spend time on the model and semantics.

## Common mistakes and debugging
- A spec written once for launch and never updated; docs describe fields that no longer exist.
- Code-first specs with no review step, so framework defaults leak into the public contract.
- Generated SDKs that throw on unknown enum values, turning every additive change into a client outage.
- Contract tests that assert the provider's entire response instead of only what the consumer uses, so they break on harmless additions.
- Debug drift with response validation in staging (log every response that does not match the spec) and Schemathesis runs in CI.

## In the interview
They probe whether you have run APIs with real consumers: how you keep spec, code, docs and SDKs in sync, how you catch breaking changes before release, and when contract testing is worth its cost.

**Model 60-second answer**: "The contract lives in an OpenAPI spec committed to the repo. I like generating it from runtime schemas so validation and spec share one source, but the generated diff is reviewed in every pull request like design-first. CI lints it with Spectral against our style guide, diffs it against the last release to block breaking changes, and fuzzes the implementation with Schemathesis. Docs, mocks and SDKs are generated from it, and SDKs handle retries, idempotency keys, pagination and unknown enum values. Between internal services with independent deploys, I add Pact consumer-driven contracts with can-i-deploy, so a provider knows exactly which change breaks which consumer. New endpoints go through a short written API review focused on the resource model and evolution."

**Follow-ups to expect**: Design-first or code-first, and why? What does a provider state mean in Pact? How do you stop a generated SDK from breaking on a new enum value? What would you put in an API style guide?

projects.architecture:
```text
client / SDK --HTTPS--> edge (TLS, coarse IP limit)
   --> API service
        auth (hashed API key -> account, scopes)
        rate limiter (token bucket: Redis Lua, Postgres fallback, fail open)
        version pinning (Stripe-Version style header or account default)
        request transforms  old -> latest
        handlers (zod validation, problem+json errors)
        idempotency (keys table in same tx as side effect)
        response transforms latest -> old
   --> Postgres (accounts, api_keys, orders, payments, idempotency_keys, outbox)
   --> outbox relay --> webhook dispatcher (signed, retries with jitter, DLQ)

CI: zod schemas -> openapi.yaml -> Spectral lint -> oasdiff vs last release
    -> SDK generation -> Pact verification -> Schemathesis fuzz
```
Key decisions: the idempotency record and the business write share one Postgres transaction; Redis is an optimisation with a Postgres fallback; the core handlers only know the latest shape and dated transforms serve older versions; every list endpoint uses keyset cursors; webhooks go through a transactional outbox so an event is never sent for a rolled-back write.

deepDives.title: Idempotency under concurrency and crashes
deepDives.body:
The naive version (check Redis for the key, run the handler, store the response) has two races. Two concurrent requests with the same key both see "not found" and both execute. And a crash after the payment insert but before storing the response leaves a charged customer and no record, so the retry charges again.

The fix is to make the key row and the business write one atomic unit:

```text
BEGIN
  INSERT idempotency_keys (account, key, hash, locked_at) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
  if conflict: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE
      hash differs        -> 422
      response is null    -> 409 (in progress)
      else                -> return saved response
  INSERT payment ...
  UPDATE idempotency_keys SET response = ...
COMMIT
```

The primary key on (account, key) serialises concurrent attempts; the transaction guarantees the payment exists if and only if the saved response exists. When the handler calls an external processor, one transaction cannot span it, so split the work into recovery points (as in Brandur Leach's design): record "started", call the processor with our own idempotency key, record "charged", then finish. A background job resumes keys stuck at a recovery point. Test it with 50 concurrent requests and with a process kill between steps.

deepDives.title: Rate limiting that is fair, atomic and survivable
deepDives.body:
Per-key token buckets live in Redis as a hash of tokens and last-refill time. A Lua script computes the refill, takes the cost and writes back atomically, so concurrent requests on different instances cannot both spend the last token. Costs are weighted (a list call costs more than a read), and two limits stack: per key and per account, so one customer cannot exhaust capacity by creating many keys.

Failure modes decide the design. If Redis times out (budget: a few milliseconds), the limiter falls back to a local in-memory bucket sized at the per-instance share of the limit, and the API keeps serving; login and key-creation limits fail closed instead. Clients see `429` with `Retry-After` and budget headers on every response so well-behaved SDKs can pace themselves. Per-client limits do not protect against total overload, so a separate concurrency limiter sheds low-priority work when the database pool is saturated, returning `503`. Measure: allowed versus rejected per key, limiter latency and fallback activations.

deepDives.title: Versioning with backwards transforms
Keeping the contract honest in CI
deepDives.body:
The spec is generated from the same zod schemas the handlers validate with, then committed. CI runs four gates on every pull request:

1. **Spectral** with a house ruleset: snake_case fields, plural collection paths, cursor pagination parameters on list operations, problem+json for 4xx and 5xx, an `Idempotency-Key` header on every POST.
2. **oasdiff** against the spec of the last released tag; removals, type changes and new required request fields fail unless the change is registered as a version change module.
3. **Pact** verification of the sample consumer's contracts against the running provider with seeded provider states.
4. **Schemathesis** fuzzing a disposable instance, failing on any 500 or response that does not match the spec.

The SDK is regenerated on merge, and its tests include a fixture with an unknown enum value and an unknown field to prove forward compatibility.
